column1: What is the Liar Paradox and why does it resist truth-value assignment?
column2: The sentence L: 'This statement is false.' If L is true, then it is false; if L is false, then it is true. The self-referential structure causes an oscillation with no stable truth value, revealing a limit on naive truth predicates in expressive languages.

column1: State Tarski's Undefinability of Truth theorem and its core mechanism.
column2: No sufficiently expressive formal language L can contain its own consistent truth predicate True(x). Using diagonalization, one constructs a sentence λ ≡ ¬True(⌜λ⌝) (⌜λ⌝ = Gödel code of λ), yielding a contradiction. This forces stratification into object language/metalanguage hierarchies.

column1: What is Russell's Paradox and what formal flaw does it expose?
column2: Define R = {x | x ∉ x} under naive (unrestricted) comprehension. Then R ∈ R implies R ∉ R, and R ∉ R implies R ∈ R — a contradiction. It exposes that unrestricted comprehension (any predicate defines a set) is inconsistent, forcing axiomatic restrictions like ZF's Separation schema.

column1: What is the key structural invariant that diagonal arguments exploit?
column2: Any proposed enumeration of an infinite set contains a constructible witness to its own incompleteness — for any claimed bijection f: ℕ → S, a diagonal construction produces an element of S provably not in the range of f.

column1: State Cantor's Theorem and its proof technique.
column2: For any set A, |A| < |P(A)| (no surjection A → P(A) exists). Proof: suppose f: A → P(A) is surjective; define D = {a ∈ A | a ∉ f(a)}. D ∈ P(A), so D = f(b) for some b. Then b ∈ D ⟺ b ∉ f(b) = D, a contradiction. Hence no such surjection exists.

column1: Define cardinal equality/comparison and state the Cantor-Bernstein-Schröder theorem.
column2: |A| = |B| iff there exists a bijection f: A → B. |A| ≤ |B| iff an injection A → B exists. CBS theorem: if |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A| (injections exist both ways), then |A| = |B| (a bijection exists).

column1: Give two examples showing Q and Z are countable despite seeming 'denser' than N.
column2: Z: interleave as 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, ... giving an explicit bijection with N. Q: arrange rationals in a 2D numerator/denominator grid and traverse diagonally (Cantor's pairing), skipping duplicates, yielding an explicit enumeration.

column1: What is the Halting Problem and what did Turing prove about it in 1936?
column2: The Halting Problem asks: given an arbitrary program and input, does it eventually halt or run forever? Turing proved no algorithm can decide this for all program/input pairs — it is undecidable, a consequence of computation's logical structure, not resource limits.

column1: List the seven components of the formal Turing machine tuple M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, q_accept, q_reject) and the role of δ.
column2: Q: finite states; Σ: input alphabet (excludes blank); Γ: tape alphabet (⊔ ∈ Γ, Σ ⊆ Γ); δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L,R} transition function (reads symbol/state, writes symbol, moves head, changes state); q0: start state; q_accept/q_reject: distinct halting states.

column1: What does it mean for a Turing machine M to 'recognize' a language L(M)?
column2: L(M) = { w ∈ Σ* | M halts and enters q_accept when started on input w }. Note this differs from 'deciding' a language, which additionally requires M to halt (accept or reject) on every input, never looping forever.

column1: What is the core self-referential mechanism behind Gödel's First Incompleteness Theorem?
column2: Using Gödel numbering (arithmetization of syntax), construct a sentence G that effectively asserts 'G is not provable in the system.' If G were provable, the system would prove a false statement (inconsistency); if ¬G were provable, the system would prove a false statement. So in a consistent system, G is true but unprovable — a truth beyond formal derivation.

column1: State Gödel's Second Incompleteness Theorem and its relation to Hilbert's program.
column2: No sufficiently powerful consistent formal system can prove its own consistency (i.e., cannot prove Con(S) within S itself). This refuted Hilbert's program, which sought a finitistic proof of the consistency of all mathematics from within a single axiomatized system.
